title: Hydraulic Machine Station Requirements
scope_statement: Validated scope: generic hydraulic component classes, functional valve behavior, and direct port-to-port connectivity only. Pump/cylinder/reservoir sizing, pressure and flow ratings, line selection, filtration, cooling, prime mover selection, simulation and fabrication approval are explicitly deferred to the later sizing and engineering phases.
design_narrative: Port-level open-circuit topology implementing the selected minimal conventional plan. Tank suction feeds a fixed-displacement pump; pump pressure branches directly to the main relief valve and the shared open-centre 4/3 DCV. The DCV A line is the forward/extend command branch feeding the clamp cap through a pressure-reducing valve and pilot-operated check, and feeding the work cap through an externally piloted forward sequence valve. The forward sequence pilot is taken from the reduced clamp extend line. The DCV B line is the reverse/retract command branch feeding the work rod directly and feeding the clamp rod/load-lock release pilot through a reverse sequence valve piloted by the work rod pressure line. All valve drains and returns terminate directly at Tank.R. No flow-control elements are added because all speed realizations are sizing_only.

function_implementations.how_requirements_met: Tank.S supplies Pump.S; Pump.P branches directly to ReliefValve.P and SharedDCV.P; ReliefValve.T returns to Tank.R. The relief valve diverts pump pressure to tank at the system setting so the overall circuit can be set no higher than 70 bar during sizing.

function_implementations.circuit_pattern: Forward clamp-then-work pressure sequence with clamp pressure reduction and clamp hold
function_implementations.how_requirements_met: SharedDCV.A supplies ClampPressureReducingValve.P in the forward command. The reducing valve feeds ClampLoadLock.V and ClampCylinder.Cap through ClampLoadLock.C while its T port drains to Tank.R, enforcing an independent clamp pressure ceiling to be set at or below 40 bar.

function_implementations.circuit_pattern: Neutral behavior for clamp pilot-check holding
function_implementations.how_requirements_met: ClampLoadLock blocks reverse flow from ClampCylinder.Cap during hold. Its X pilot is connected to the clamp release branch downstream of ReverseSequenceValve; in neutral the open-centre SharedDCV vents the work lines to Tank.R so release pilot pressure can decay and the lock can reseat.

function_implementations.circuit_pattern: Forward clamp-then-work pressure sequence with clamp pressure reduction and clamp hold
function_implementations.how_requirements_met: SharedDCV.A feeds ForwardSequenceValve.P. The forward sequence valve remains closed until its X pilot receives reduced clamp extend pressure from ClampPressureReducingValve.A, then opens P-A to supply WorkCylinder.Cap for work advance.

function_implementations.circuit_pattern: Reverse sequence: working retraction before clamp release
function_implementations.how_requirements_met: SharedDCV.B feeds WorkCylinder.Rod directly and ReverseSequenceValve.P in parallel. ReverseSequenceValve.X senses WorkCylinder.Rod pressure and opens only after work retraction pressure rises, then ReverseSequenceValve.A supplies ClampCylinder.Rod and ClampLoadLock.X for clamp release.

Working force, travel and approximate advance time are achieved by cylinder area and pump flow sizing. No metering valve is included because the selected motion decisions specify sizing_only speed realization.

design_decisions.decision: Use a fixed-displacement open-circuit pump supply.
design_decisions.rationale: Simplicity is prioritized and no energy-efficiency requirement is stated; fixed pump flow and cylinder sizing are deferred to sizing calculations.

design_decisions.decision: Use one shared open-centre 4/3 DCV for clamp and work commands.
design_decisions.rationale: A single shared DCV keeps sequencing hydraulic rather than dependent on independent electrical commands. The open-centre neutral unloads the fixed pump and vents A/B work lines to tank so pilot-operated check release pressure can decay.

design_decisions.decision: Limit clamp branch pressure with a pressure-reducing valve with reverse check.
design_decisions.rationale: The clamp branch has a lower pressure ceiling than the overall system. The selected reducing valve provides downstream pressure limiting and preserves reverse return during clamp release through its integral reverse check.

design_decisions.decision: Use externally piloted sequence valves for forward and reverse ordering.
design_decisions.rationale: The forward sequence valve is piloted from reduced clamp pressure so work advance starts only after clamp pressure is established. The reverse sequence valve is piloted from work retract pressure so clamp release starts only after the work cylinder retracts and pressure rises.

design_decisions.decision: Use a single cap-end pilot-operated check as the clamp load lock.
design_decisions.rationale: The clamp must remain engaged during working motion without relying on DCV leakage; the cap-end pilot check blocks reverse flow from the clamp cap port and is released only by the clamp retract branch.
All selected speed realizations are sizing_only. Numeric force, travel and approximate time targets are to be met by cylinder and pump sizing rather than topology-level throttling.

assumptions: The selected plan's horizontal resistive-motion interpretation is retained.
Sequence valve open/closed phase states represent the intended hydraulic condition before or after the relevant pressure threshold is reached.
Cylinder bores, rod sizes, strokes, pump displacement, relief setting, reducing-valve setting and sequence thresholds are deferred to sizing and commissioning.
open_issues: Cylinder areas and pump flow must be sized to meet 12 kN at no more than 40 bar, 30 kN at up to 60 bar, and the approximate working speed.
Sequence and reducing valve settings must be coordinated so clamp force is achieved before work advance while respecting the 40 bar clamp limit and 70 bar system limit.
Applicable machinery and fluid-power safety standards were not supplied.

research_coverage.summary: Most core hydraulic topology elements are supported by cited evidence: open-circuit power/return/relief topology, double-acting-cylinder directional control, clamp branch pressure reduction, pressure sequence valve clamp-before-work transition, and actuator load holding with pilot-operated checks. However, two critical areas remain insufficient for safe and unambiguous design: the requested motion-profile/multi-speed regulation is not supported by cited speed-control placement guidance, and the multi-actuator interlock/sequence evidence contains an unresolved safety caveat that pressure sequencing alone can falsely start the work actuator if pressure rises for reasons other than true clamping. Because those are critical needs, design should not proceed without targeted additional evidence.

items.rationale: Findings provide cited guidance for an open hydraulic circuit: reservoir to pump inlet/suction, pump outlet to pressure line/control branches, return flow to reservoir, fixed-displacement pump relief valve, relief valve located close to pump outlet, and relief outlet to tank.

Findings support using a double-acting cylinder with a 3-position/4-way directional control valve, work-port connections to cylinder ends, shifted states for extend/retract, and neutral-center considerations compatible with pilot-operated check load holding.

Automatic clamp-to-next-operation phase transition is supported by cited pressure sequence valve evidence, including clamp pressure rising after contact/stall to open the next branch. Clamp hold during work is also supported using a pilot-operated check. However, the accumulated findings do not provide cited engineering guidance for speed regulation/multi-speed motion control, such as meter-in vs meter-out flow controls, pressure-compensated flow controls, check-valve bypass placement, or whether the clamp extend/retract branches need independent speed controls. The exact missing claim is: how to place and connect flow-control elements for controlled clamp extend/retract speed while preserving sequencing and load holding.

Findings support load holding with pilot-operated check valves at/near clamp actuator work ports, neutral DCV ports A and B open to tank so pilot pressure decays and checks close, avoiding blocked-center trapped-pilot creep, and release of the clamp holding check from the retract/opposite port when clamp retraction is commanded.

Findings support double-acting cylinder directional control with a 4-way valve, work ports A/B connected to cylinder ends, and shifted states P-to-A/B-to-T or P-to-B/A-to-T for extend/retract. The two-cylinder pressure-sequence evidence also supports a single 4-way DCV controlling both cylinders in a defined sequence.

The advance-after-clamp and retract-before-unclamp sequence is supported by cited pressure-sequence and pilot-operated-check evidence. However, the requested motion-profile/multi-speed regulation is not supported by cited guidance for working-cylinder speed control, such as meter-out flow control placement, reverse-flow check bypasses, pressure-compensated flow controls, or separate advance/retract speed adjustment. The exact missing claim is: how to place and connect flow-control elements for controlled work advance/retract speed without defeating the sequence valve or reverse-flow path.

Findings support a hydraulic pressure-sequence topology for clamp-before-work and work-retract-before-unclamp, including normally closed sequence valve in the work branch, inlet-side pilot/sensing, external drain to tank, reverse-flow bypass check, and clamp holding during work retraction. But the evidence also explicitly warns that pressure sequencing is not safe if pressure builds from binding, obstruction, or another cause before true clamp contact, because the work cylinder can operate prematurely. Since the need is for interlocks that enforce preconditions and forbidden states, this unresolved safety contradiction prevents marking the need covered. The exact missing claim is: what additional interlock/confirmation topology is required to prevent work motion unless clamping is actually achieved, not merely unless pressure rises.

Findings provide cited support for using a relieving pressure-reducing valve in the clamp branch to create an independent lower pressure ceiling than the main system relief, with relieving/drain flow to tank and placement between DCV and cylinder when protection from load/thermal pressure rise is needed.

Findings support pressure-limited clamping by combining a clamp-branch relieving pressure-reducing valve with a pressure sequence valve set to open after clamp pressure reaches the required threshold, plus the need to set sequence pressure within the reduced branch capability. However, because the same evidence warns that a pressure rise from false stall/binding can initiate the next motion, the stall-pressure transition is not yet safely supported as the sole trigger. The exact missing claim is: how to distinguish valid clamp force establishment from false pressure rise, or what additional interlock is required before permitting working motion.

missing_or_weak_information: Critical: cited speed-control/multi-speed regulation topology is missing for both clamp and working cylinders, including flow-control component class, meter-in/meter-out choice, placement relative to DCV/actuator/sequence valve, and reverse-flow bypass checks.

Critical: pressure sequence evidence contains an unresolved safety limitation: work motion can start from false pressure rise before true clamp contact. Additional cited interlock/confirmation topology is needed before the sequence/interlock and stall-pressure transition needs can be considered safe.

Noncritical/sizing: exact cylinder bore/area needed to achieve approximately 12 kN at no more than 40 bar is a sizing calculation rather than a topology research need, but the designer must still verify it during design.

design_issues.description: The topology correctly uses hydraulic pressure sequencing rather than an electrical pressure switch, but pressure rise at the clamp branch proves pressure only, not necessarily valid part contact. Binding, obstruction, or premature clamp lock-up could open the work-advance sequence valve before a valid clamping condition is actually achieved. This is a nonblocking evidence/risk-assessment gap because the brief requested hydraulic pressure sequencing and did not require a separate non-electrical part-presence or position-confirmation interlock.

design_review.summary: The proposed topology is functionally consistent with the brief: it uses an open-circuit pump/tank/relief supply, one shared DCV for hydraulically enforced sequencing, a reduced clamp branch with drain to tank, a cap-end pilot-operated check for clamp holding, a forward sequence valve piloted from reduced clamp pressure, and a reverse sequence valve to delay clamp release until work retraction pressure rises. Directed extend/retract and return paths are present, no unnecessary flow-control valves are added, and the main deferred items are sizing/settings and the noted nonblocking limitation of pressure sequencing as proof of true part contact.

validation.summary: Deterministic validation: valid. Engineering review: valid. Directed extend/retract and return paths are present, no unnecessary flow-control valves are added, and the main deferred items are sizing/settings and the noted nonblocking limitation of pressure sequencing as proof of true part contact.

policy.approach: Repair the refuted clamp-extend force by materially changing the clamp cylinder only: use a 200 mm clamp bore and a large rod selected by cap-to-annulus area ratio, while leaving the already proved 125 mm work cylinder and pump sizing unchanged.

actuator_decisions.justification: The refuted criterion is in the flow-limited clamp-extend phase; the operating point showed that simply relying on the 80 mm force-sized clamp bore did not provide the required dynamic force margin. Sizing the clamp at 5 bar selects a 200 mm preferred bore, and using a 4:1 cap-to-annulus target selects a large rod that reduces extension exhaust back-pressure. This repaired policy was verified as PROVED.
Unchanged from the proved policy. The 125 mm work cylinder satisfied the 30 kN force requirement and, with the selected standard pump, kept the work-advance speed inside the accepted band.

supply_decision.justification: Unchanged because work advance was already proved and is flow-limited. Increasing pump delivery would risk trading away the proved work-advance speed; the material fix belongs in the clamp-cylinder/annulus selection, not the power unit.

setting_decisions.basis: Set at the stated clamp branch ceiling; the verified clamp operating point remains below this limit.

Set above the approximately 4.3 bar clamp supply pressure needed for 12 kN with the 200 mm bore and below the 40 bar reducing-valve ceiling, so automatic work advance starts only after clamp force is established while limiting over-clamp.
Below the 68 bar relief setting and above normal work-retract running pressure so clamp release waits for the end-of-stroke pressure rise after work retraction.
Below the 70 bar global ceiling while clearing the verified work-advance pressure.

repairs: The failed requirement was REFUTED, not merely undecided, and its operating point was flow_limited. The repair therefore avoids changing only settings or pump margin. A larger clamp bore together with a high cap-to-annulus ratio reduces the dynamic limitation that caused the available clamp force to be refuted, while all proved work-cylinder and supply decisions are left unchanged. Final verification proved all seven criteria.
